summary: N. A. Jayawickrama worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and linguistics. He served as a professor at the University of Ceylon (attested 1974) and the Postgraduate Institute of Pali and Buddhist Studies.

N. Aiyaswami Sastri studied at Madras Sanskrit College and Visva-Bharati University, working in Indology and Buddhist studies. He held posts as professor at Sri Venkateswara Oriental College (attested 1940) and Visva-Bharati University (attested 1971), and reader at Sri Venkateswara Oriental Research Institute.
N. D. Mironov was an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1902–1903) and under Heinrich Hübschmann (~1902–1903) and Hermann Jacobi (~1903–1904).
Working in computational fields and Indology, N. J. Karthika earned a Ph.D. from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay and held a post there.

N. Lakshminarayana Rao worked in Indology and history and archaeology. He served as Government Epigraphist for India at the Archaeological Survey of India and was Special Officer (Epigraphy) for the Government of India in 1956.
N. R. Bhatt worked in Indology. He held a post at the French Institute of Pondicherry and was a member of the École française d'Extrême-Orient (attested 1966).

Specializing in history, archaeology, and Indology, N. S. Ramachandra Murthy was an Epigraphy Assistant in the Andhra Pradesh Department of Archaeology and Museums and retired as Professor of Indian History and Archaeology at Sri Venkateswara University.

Active in Indology and philosophy, N. S. Ramanuja Tatacharya was a researcher at the French Institute of Pondicherry (~1979–1989) and Vice Chancellor of the National Sanskrit University from 1989 to 1994.
N. Taher is an archaeologist who succeeded K. K. Muhammed to serve as head of the Bhopal circle at the Archaeological Survey of India.

Active in Indology and philosophy, N. Veezhinathan earned a PhD from Savitribai Phule Pune University (-1964), studying under A. Sankaran, T. M. P. Mahadevan, and T. S. Srinivasa Sastri. He worked at Deccan College and the University of Madras.

N. Venkataramanayya studied under Ferrand E. Corley and worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as Reader in Indian History at the University of Madras (attested 1957) and Deputy Director for Epigraphy for Andhra Pradesh.

Nae Ionescu was a philosopher and religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Bucharest (~1908–1912) and the universities of Göttingen (~1913–1914) and Munich (~1916–1919). He held a post at the University of Bucharest (~1919–1938).
Working in Indology and philosophy, Nagin J. Shah succeeded Dalsukh Malvania and served as Acting Director of the L.D. Institute of Indology (attested 1968).

Active in Buddhist studies and Indology, Nalinaksha Dutt earned degrees from the University of Calcutta and the University of London. He was Head of Pali at Calcutta (~1921–1958) and served as President of The Asiatic Society (1959–1961).

Indologist Nalini Balbir studied under Colette Caillat (~1974–1980). She held posts at the CNRS (1982–1988), Sorbonne Nouvelle University (professor from 1988), INALCO (~1988–2020), EPHE (Directeur d'Études from 2000), and Pali Text Society (~2012).
Working in religious studies, philosophy, and Indology, Nalini Devdas earned a PhD at Concordia University under Leslie Orr and studied with several teachers. She held a post at Carleton University.

Nam-lin Hur studied at the University of Tokyo and under Helen Hardacre, Martin Collcutt, and Fumio Tamamuro. A postdoctoral fellow at Harvard, he became professor of Japanese history and religious culture at the University of British Columbia (attested 2000).

Naman P. Ahuja earned a doctorate from SOAS University of London in history, archaeology, and Indology. He was appointed Professor of Indian Art and Architecture at Jawaharlal Nehru University (attested 2018).

Namgyal Rinpoche studied at the University of Michigan, Jarvis Baptist Seminary, and under teachers including Sayadaw U Thila Wunta and the 16th Karmapa. Active in Buddhist and religious studies, he founded Kagyu Samye Ling and the Dharma Centre of Canada.

Namio Egami studied at the University of Tokyo (~1927–1930) and worked in history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He held a post at the University of Tokyo (~1948–1967) and directed the Ancient Orient Museum (~1978–2002).
